title: The Revival, patience and gratitude
hookLine: faith is two halves: patience and gratitude
tomorrow: why would a grandmother calmly plan her own funeral?

cards: Your phone buzzes twice in the same hour. The first message: bad news, the kind that makes your stomach drop. The second: good news, the kind that makes you laugh out loud in public.

Now you're holding both, and they don't cancel out. What do you do with a day like that? Al-Ghazali gives a whole book of the Revival to exactly this pair, and he opens it with a saying he quotes: faith is two halves.
Half is patience. Half is gratitude.

teach.b: Patience, sabr, is holding steady under what hurts: not pretending it doesn't, but not letting it knock you off your feet.
Gratitude, shukr, is noticing what's been given and letting it turn you toward the Giver. Al-Ghazali's point is that a person of faith needs both, the way a body needs two hands.
There's a hadith in Sahih Muslim that says it plainly, and it's one worth repeating to a friend.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said the affair of the believer is a wonder: if something good comes, they're grateful, and that's good for them; if harm comes, they're patient, and that's good for them too.
Every situation has a half that fits it. The Qur'an asks people to seek help in patience and in prayer, in Pickthall's words, "Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast."
Now a quieter point in this book.
Al-Ghazali doesn't keep the halves in separate rooms. Hard days hold small gifts to be thankful for; good days ask for patience too, to stay humble and not grab.
So on a day with two buzzes, you don't have to pick one feeling. You can hold the hard news with one hand, steady, and the good news with the other, open.

how: Muslims may answer hard news with patience, saying they belong to God and return to Him, and good news with alhamdulillah; al-Ghazali's book on patience and gratitude is read in study circles as a guide to both.

games.q: you win the scholarship, and the same day your best friend doesn't. you want to celebrate, and you want to be kind. what fits the two halves?
o: hide your gratitude completely so nobody feels bad.
celebrate loudly; your good news doesn't need any patience.

games.why: al-Ghazali keeps the halves together: a good day still asks for patience, to stay humble and not grab.

practice: Rest your left hand closed and still on your knee: let it hold one hard thing you're carrying, without squeezing. Turn your right hand palm up, and on its fingers count small gifts from today, a meal, a voice, a warm room.
Sit with both hands like that.

wordCard.voice: The Revival, again: here its book on patience and gratitude, the two halves of faith, held together.

carryVoice: Your line: two halves, one steady hand and one open hand. Whatever today brings, it fits one of them.
